question: A market summary states that three customer segments account for 45, 38 and 29 percent of revenue. The analyst notices the three add to more than a hundred. What should she conclude?
options: A) That the largest segment is the one in error, since a figure of 45 percent is the least likely of the three to be right.
B) That rounding explains the excess, so the figures can be used once each one is rounded to the nearest whole number.
C) That the segments must overlap, so the summary is correct and needs only a footnote explaining the overlap to readers.
D) That the numeric section is unreliable as a whole, and every figure in it needs checking against the source data.
correct_answers: D) That the numeric section is unreliable as a whole, and every figure in it needs checking against the source data.
explanations: Nothing identifies which figure is wrong. Picking one on the basis of its size is a guess, and the other two may be equally unfounded.
Rounding moves totals by a point or two at most. A twelve-point excess is far outside what rounding can produce, so this explanation does not fit the evidence.
Overlapping segments are possible, but that is an assumption invented to rescue the numbers. If overlap were intended the summary would have to say so, and it does not.

Correct. The inconsistency shows that the figures were not derived from a single reconciled source, which says nothing reassuring about any individual number. One visible contradiction is a reason to re-check the whole set.
